metadata.title: Probate  Part 3,  "Wording of Wills"  by James Tanner
metadata.author: BYU Library Family History Center
metadata.shortDescription: This is the next installment of the 9 part Probate Series.

segments.text: welcome to the ins and outs of probate
virginie ologist this segment is called
understanding the language of a will
this is part of an ongoing series of
nine videos concerning probate all of
these videos will it be available on the
Brigham Young University family history
youtube families to library YouTube
channel the language of a will is very
conservative if you were to read a will
today you would see language that was
similar to a wheel written in the 1700s
it is not impossible that you would find
the same phrases and it is probable that
you would see the same structure no
matter how difficult the handwriting may
appear to be most of the wheels have a
standard format and you can almost
always look for the same words and
phrases in an old will as you will find
in a brand new will the law in the
United States is based on a principle
called starry decisis this comes from
the English common law the term means
let the lost and and that means that the
courts rely on prior court decisions to
determine how to apply the law in the
current case when I refer to the
corridor usually am referring to the
judge so the judge in the case will make
a decision a decision based on prior law
using prior case law assures that
everyone that everyone that the law will
be applied consistently the process of
representing a client in corde involves
informing the court about how previous
cases you know that are similar have
been decided so an attorney will write
what is called a brief or a memorandum
to the court arguing that the court
should decide their clients or his or
her client
case consistent with cases that are
cited however it's clear that there's
usually someone on the opposite side who
is making a different and exactly
opposite argument so the court has to
sort out which of the case is applied to
this particular mat to the particular
matter before the court it's a little
bit different in the probate court
action with concerning a will there is
not all with someone on the opposite
side most of the probate cases are
unopposed but there are many times when
probate cases involve disagreements
among the heirs or even issues raised by
third parties such as creditors in these
cases the court treats the will contest
matter or the probate matter just as
they would any other lawsuit and the
lawyers need to cite case already
unfortunately the law doesn't exactly
work all the same ways all the time and
so it's as applied it changes the
problem I guess you call it the break or
the constraint on the law changing too
rapidly is the changes in the wording of
a will can result in changes as the way
as to the way is the law is applied to
the will so the courts have to decide if
the new what the new language means and
how it relates to previous rulings and
how it will affect the law in the future
of course wills use language that may be
unfamiliar these are not the words you'd
have on your grade school spelling test
you may have to work slowly at first
understand what's being said in the will
very important to focus on each word if
you don't know the meaning of the word
look it up you may need to use a
reference book or an online source to
decipher the terms and figure out who
got what
one of the basic books is the black's
law dictionary which I mentioned in a
previous segment of this video you can
see that online and do a search for
black's law dictionary there's many
websites such as the law dictionary
websites cited here where that use
black's law dictionary to define legal
terms the other good source is the
Internet Archive that's archive.org and
they have a complete text of the 6th
edition available for searching now each
of the wheel is broken each will is
broken down into some common provisions
the important thing to understand that
these particular provisions are
necessary and required for a valid will
the first is a statement of the identity
of the testator testator is the person
making the will next is a statement of
the testator's intent to make a will
this is called testamentary intent and
that and the person making a whale has
to clearly state they want to dispose of
their property upon their demise or upon
their death next is a statement setting
forth the details of the family or the
people who will inherit the property
usually called the heirs could be called
heirs and assigns and a whole bunch of
other words that they basically boil
down to the people who get the property
next in line is the appointment of an
executor of personal representative this
depends on the jurisdiction the wording
if person has a will the person
administering the will is called an
executor if there is no will if it's in
testing rather than a test state action
then the person is an administrator in
some jurisdictions in the United States
both are referred to by the term
personal representative there's some
additional common provision so will the
will can contain
directions to the executor or personal
representative things that they would
like to see happen that the testator
would like to see happen you can also
find a bequest a devise or grant of the
assets of the estate each of those words
have a restricted legal meaning
depending on the particular state they
could be construed but it's not unusual
to see all three of them put together in
that in the form of i bequeath devise
and grant or something of that nature
there's also a possibility that the
testator will put in some special
provisions for the devisees for those
who are receiving specific requests
these things usually deal with specific
items of personal property any other
instructions are also included for
example care of minor children or the
maintenance of a spouse last it's
necessary to have a signature and
witnesses usually two witnesses well
that's the end of this one thanks for
watching there will be a number of
additional segments up to nine in this
series and we hope that you can follow
all of them
